# Environments and Tool Interfaces {#sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"We shape our tools and thereafter they shape us."*
>
> --- John Culkin, *Saturday Review* (1967) [@Culkin1967Schoolman]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** John Culkin, an American media scholar writing to explain Marshall McLuhan's ideas, observed that tools reshape how people work. The line is often credited to McLuhan, but it is Culkin's, a small provenance lesson of its own. An architecture tool also shapes what an AI method can change and what an architect can observe. Those limits must be explicit when the method acts through the tool.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
How do we bridge the semantic gap between an AI's abstract intent and the messy, stateful reality of computer architecture tools to create a reliable design environment?
:::

@sec-data-representations-world-models established how design state is represented to an AI method, and @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization introduced the search, generation, and optimization roles that act on it. However, a method's proposals are useless in a vacuum. Once an agent proposes a design change (whether sizing a new cache hierarchy via Bayesian Optimization or proposing a new prefetcher via an LLM) it must actually execute that intent to gather evidence. This chapter builds the Implement stage's machinery: the execution environment.

In a traditional workflow, the architect manually builds the design, launches a simulator like gem5, a cycle-level architectural simulator, or Ramulator, a main memory simulator. The architect then parses the console output and debugs any segmentation faults or license errors. Scaling AI-driven design requires replacing human-in-the-loop debugging with direct, programmatic agent-tool interactions. However, giving an AI permission to execute a shell script is not an environment.

This chapter connects an AI's abstract intent to the stateful reality of computer architecture and Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools. We will define how to structure the read, action, and return paths, handle asynchronous execution, distinguish between tool crashes and design failures, and distill sprawling simulation logs into dense semantic observations.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Analyze the structural friction between human-centric interactive toolchains and deterministic AI interfaces to identify failure modes in automated hardware design workflows.
- Design log-to-semantic parsing layers that extract structured observation vectors from unstructured hardware telemetry and execution logs.
- Evaluate the limitations of synchronous reinforcement learning environment wrappers when interfacing with long-running, license-constrained architectural simulators.
- Synthesize cloud-native desired-state reconciliation and bioinformatics dataflow isolation to decouple high-level AI intent from tool execution mechanics.

:::

## The Human–API Mismatch

In modern machine learning, an agent interacts with an environment such as an OpenAI Gym[^fn-openai-gym-c06] simulation through a clean, synchronous loop. It takes an action, and the environment returns a new state and a dense scalar reward.

[^fn-openai-gym-c06]: **OpenAI Gym**: The de facto standard reinforcement-learning environment API, in which an agent calls a step function with an action and receives the next state and a scalar reward. Its successor library, Gymnasium, keeps the same interface contract.

Hardware tools were built for humans, not APIs. For decades, architecture tools such as CACTI [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI], DRAMSys [@WeisEtAl2021DRAMSys], or gem5 were engineered around manual workflows, assuming an architect who can read dense log files, debug build errors interactively, and interpret color-coded waveforms. Modifying a real design means navigating a disconnected stack. Inserting a custom vector block into an XR subsystem requires modifying Chisel, changing linker scripts, and hacking a Device Tree Blob (DTB). Forcing these messy realities into a standard ML environment loop without exposing their low-level details prevents the human architect from verifying physical constraints like timing and power.

This legacy breaks the familiar ML environment paradigm, creating a **semantic gap**. That gap separates the high-level semantic intent of a design ("increase the cache size to improve hit rate") from the low-level, unstructured mechanics of the tool itself. Instead of returning a simple scalar reward, EDA tools return gigabytes of unparsed logs, crash silently, or hang for days. The mismatch grows as design moves down the stack. The EDA tools at the bottom rely heavily on the tacit knowledge of physical design engineers to interpret unroutable netlists, whereas an AI system requires fully explicit, programmatic interfaces.

Foundation models interact most reliably with external software through strict, typed APIs rather than unconstrained shell commands. Constraining generation to a typed, retrieved API surface sharply cuts the argument hallucinations that raw shell access invites [@PatilEtAl2024Gorilla]. Tool-use research points the same way. Toolformer trains a model to invoke typed APIs for subtasks it cannot perform reliably on its own [@SchickEtAl2023Toolformer], and ReAct interleaves reasoning with tool calls so the model consumes each observation before choosing its next action [@YaoEtAl2023ReAct]. This maps directly to the architectural domain. While "computer use" models can visually parse GUIs and move a mouse, relying on visual GUI automation for architecture design is brittle and computationally inefficient; on real desktop tasks the strongest such agents finish only a small fraction of what a human completes [@XieEtAl2024OSWorld]. Because of this, system intent, a GUI, and simple permission to call a tool are insufficient for real architecture work. Strict API boundaries instead of raw shell access keep control with the human architect, who can bound the AI's legal actions before spending cluster hours on unroutable silicon.

A second mismatch is the brownfield reality. Most AI research focuses on greenfield design, generating a brand new core or accelerator from a blank slate. In industry, however, most of an architect's job is brownfield work [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. This involves integrating legacy IP blocks, wrangling proprietary vendor protocols, and navigating undocumented system buses. To bridge this gap, the environment must expose structured hardware description standards. However, not all standards are equal. IP-XACT is a notoriously bloated XML standard; feeding raw IP-XACT to a generative model will immediately exhaust its context window with boilerplate. The environment's "Read Path" must distill heavy XML standards into lightweight JSON or YAML representations, whereas denser formats like SystemRDL might be read natively. This distillation allows the agent to programmatically discover and memory-map legacy AXI or TileLink interfaces without relying on unstructured text datasheets. If an AI agent cannot successfully wire up a black-box memory controller to a modern coherency fabric, it cannot design a real System-on-Chip. The environment must expose interfaces for both generating new IP and integrating messy, opaque legacy components.

::: {.callout-war-story title="The black-box memory controller"}
**The claim.** A physical design team integrating a legacy, black-box memory controller relied on the vendor's provided PDF datasheet to establish timing constraints and protocol behaviors, trusting the text as ground truth.

**The gap.** The PDF timing diagrams did not match the actual RTL behavior under specific burst conditions. Because the interface was documented in unstructured text rather than a machine-readable, interrogatable format, the discrepancy bypassed automated checks. The mismatch was only discovered after fabrication, causing a multi-million dollar tape-out delay.

**The lesson.** This perfectly illustrates why AI needs programmatic, interrogatable hardware interfaces rather than text-based manuals. When integrating legacy IP, relying on unstructured documentation leads to catastrophic integration failures.
:::

Recall the **Lighthouse prompt** introduced in @sec-moonshot. The prompt asks to design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an XR platform. To tackle a system of this complexity, an AI agent relies on an overarching generator framework like Chipyard [@chipyard], which serves as the logical engine to emit the RISC-V SoC. An AI agent working this prompt might formulate a high-level system intent to maximize spatial tracking throughput within the strict 3 W TDP thermal envelope required for an untethered XR headset. The candidate change, inserting a custom vector-capable accelerator block into the Chipyard-generated RISC-V subsystem, is not executable as one simple function call. An agent cannot merely instantiate the block; it must resolve bandwidth contention on the TileLink or AXI interconnect between the new spatial tracking accelerator and the high-bandwidth XR display controller. To handle the bursty, streaming point-cloud data from the headset's camera sensors without thrashing the core's working set, the agent might need to propose resizing the L2 cache or adding a specialized prefetcher. Furthermore, it must update the memory-mapped IO (MMIO) and Device Tree Blob (DTB) so the XR OS and drivers actually recognize the new vector block, connecting the hardware change to the software stack.

A compiler must successfully emit the right memory mapping for the tensor instructions. The hardware configuration must instantiate the block. The RTL generator must pass simulation. Finally, the EDA flow must synthesize the design to check for routing congestion in the 3 nm layout. Each tool call can return exit code 0 while the Lighthouse architecture proposal itself remains unevaluated or logically broken.

Tool meaning depends on fixed context, legal actions, software and hardware specifications, tool versions, permissions, execution conditions, and explicitly defined failure behaviors. Two studies can call the exact same Ramulator instance while operating in different environments because their actions, workloads, constraints, and observation meanings differ. A computational method cannot infer these context dependencies via intuition. It requires the environment to explicitly expose what actions are permitted, what the tool returns, which states are invalid, and which runs can be repeated. Basic tool permissions are not enough, and the tools themselves compound the problem.

An AI requires fast, deterministic APIs, but hardware design relies on slow, stateful, and expensive legacy software. The environment sits between them. It gives the AI enough autonomy to explore the design space at scale while enforcing strict rules through permissions, budgets, and interface schemas. These rules ensure the agent does not propose physically impossible designs or waste compute time on broken Electronic Design Automation (EDA) runs.

## Balancing Architecture Environments

Hardware design is bound by tight time and compute constraints. Unlike software environments that can execute thousands of iterations per second, architecture tools are locked behind expensive licenses and days-long job queues. The compute required for a single physical design run is orders of magnitude slower and more expensive than an AI model's inference pass. As fidelity increases toward silicon, the sample budget shrinks exponentially from millions of cheap functional checks to handfuls of expensive layout runs.

### The Multi-Fidelity Ladder

To navigate this economic reality, we can look to the robotics community's approach of sim-to-real transfer. Rather than training a robotic arm directly in the physical world, which is slow and risks damaging hardware, researchers train the agent in a fast physics simulator and transfer the learned policy to the real robot [@OpenAI2019Rubik]. Architecture benefits from a similar pipeline by working across a multi-fidelity spectrum (@tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum). The simulator is not a single tool, but a ladder.

At the top are fast analytical models (ISA-level or spreadsheet models) that act as the "Sim", screening millions of candidates in seconds. In the middle are Cycle-Accurate C++ simulators, like gem5, that model timing but abstract physics. At the bottom are RTL synthesis and VLSI physical design tools, the "Real", that enforce true physical laws like power, timing, and routing congestion.

An architecture environment must allow an agent to move systematically between these levels (@fig-simulator-tax). This requires managing significant mechanical friction. For instance, the environment must manage **trace provenance**: if an AI mutates a core's branch predictor, pre-recorded memory traces become structurally invalid because speculative execution paths change. The environment must be configured to determine when to regenerate functional traces versus when to safely replay them. Furthermore, the environment must abstract **checkpointing and workload warm-up**. An AI agent running full-system gem5 cannot afford to simulate Linux booting on every iteration, nor should it optimize a cache based on cold-misses during OS boot. The environment API must abstract Region of Interest (ROI) fast-forwarding so the AI is rewarded on steady-state behavior, not initialization noise. Because navigating this ladder requires balancing conflicting physical limits, hardware specialization tightly couples the stack.

| **Fidelity Level** | **Example Tools** | **Speed** | **Physical Laws Enforced** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analytical | Spreadsheet, CACTI-class models | Near-instant (no execution) | None (closed-form estimates) |
| Functional / ISA | Spike, QEMU | ~30x slowdown | None (execution only) |
| Cycle-Approximate | ZSim [@ZSim], Sniper [@Sniper] | ~1,000x slowdown | Structural pipeline abstractions |
| Cycle-Accurate | gem5 (O3) | ~15,000x slowdown | Detailed timing, abstract physics |
| RTL Simulation | Verilator  | ~30,000x slowdown | Full logic behavior |
| FPGA Emulation | FireSim | ~20x slowdown | Full logic, mapped to FPGA fabric |
| Physical Design | Yosys [@Yosys], OpenROAD  | Hours to Days | Power, Timing, Routing, DRC |

: **Fidelity trades against speed.** An agent climbs this ladder as design candidates mature, paying more per observation as fidelity rises, except where an FPGA buys the speed back at the cost of dedicated hardware. {#tbl-multi-fidelity-spectrum tbl-colwidths="[20,25,20,35]"}

```{python}
#| label: fig-simulator-tax
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **The simulator tax: fidelity costs orders of magnitude, unless you burn an FPGA.** Representative slowdown of each architecture-evaluation approach relative to a roughly 3 GHz core. Software simulation slows by four to five orders of magnitude as fidelity rises toward cycle-accurate and RTL detail; FPGA-accelerated emulation stays within about twenty times real time, at the cost of dedicated hardware. Figures are order-of-magnitude and workload- and configuration-dependent.
#| out-width: "92%"
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal log chart of simulation slowdown versus real hardware across six approaches. Native silicon is one times. FPGA emulation (FireSim) is about twenty times slower. Functional or ISA simulation is about thirty times. Cycle-approximate simulation (ZSim, Sniper) is about one thousand times. Cycle-accurate simulation (gem5) is about fifteen thousand times. RTL simulation (Verilator) is about thirty thousand times slower."

import csv
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Data: representative simulation throughput per fidelity rung, synthesized from
# primary sources and expressed as slowdown versus a ~3 GHz core. CPU-sim rungs
# count instructions, RTL/FPGA rungs count cycles (~comparable at IPC ~1). Anchors:
# ZSim (Sanchez & Kozyrakis 2013), gem5-class ~200 KIPS ,
# Verilator (Chipyard), FireSim. Order-of-magnitude,
# workload/config/host dependent. Accessed 2026-07-19.
# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter5-simulator-tax.csv
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
rungs = []
with open(_root / "data" / "source-receipts" / "chapter5-simulator-tax.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    for d in csv.DictReader(fh):
        rungs.append({"rung": d["rung"], "example": d["example"], "slow": float(d["slowdown_vs_silicon"])})

kind = {"Native silicon": COLORS["workload"], "FPGA emulation": COLORS["evidence"]}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 3.3))
n = len(rungs)
for i, r in enumerate(rungs):
    y = n - 1 - i
    color = kind.get(r["rung"], COLORS["methods"])
    slow = r["slow"]
    ax.hlines(y, 1, max(slow, 1.02), color=color, lw=2.4, zorder=2)
    ax.scatter([max(slow, 1.02)], [y], s=46, color=color, edgecolor=color, zorder=3)
    tag = "1× (real time)" if slow < 1.5 else f"~{slow:,.0f}× slower"
    ax.text(max(slow, 1.02) * 1.35, y + 0.02, tag, va="center", ha="left", fontsize=6.0, fontweight="bold", color=color)
    ax.text(1.05, y + 0.34, r["rung"], va="center", ha="left", fontsize=7.0, fontweight="bold", color=COLORS["ink"])
    ax.text(1.05, y - 0.30, r["example"], va="center", ha="left", fontsize=5.4, color=COLORS["muted"])
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(1, 6e5)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, n - 0.2)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("Slowdown versus real hardware (log)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xticks([1, 1e1, 1e2, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5])
ax.set_xticklabels(["1×", "10×", "100×", "1,000×", "10,000×", "100,000×"], fontsize=6.2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.2, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right", "left"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(axis="x", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.02, right=0.985, top=0.97, bottom=0.14)
plt.show()
```

The rungs are orders of magnitude apart. A cycle-accurate or RTL run is ten thousand to thirty thousand times slower than the silicon it models, so an agent that optimizes for high-fidelity evidence can afford only a handful of samples; FPGA emulation buys the speed back only by committing dedicated hardware. That exponential cost turns climbing the ladder into a design decision in its own right.

Hardware specialization tightly couples the stack. Optimizing one parameter (like dataflow) cascades into breaking constraints across siloed simulation tools (thermal, synthesis, compilation). This coupled constraint problem is not unique to architecture. In aerospace engineering, designing an aircraft requires balancing aerodynamics, structures, and acoustics [@Sobieski1998BLISS]. Instead of building a single monolithic simulator, aerospace multidisciplinary design optimization (MDO) orchestrates fast *surrogate models* for broad exploration, reserving expensive physics simulators for final verification. AI in computer architecture should similarly orchestrate existing tools rather than replace them.

AI should act as an architectural control plane. Rather than just generating scripts, it must take declarative intent, measure actual state from simulators and EDA tools, and issue compensating actions, such as shrinking a cache to fix a thermal violation. ChatEDA demonstrates one realization of this pattern, decomposing a natural-language design intent into subtasks that an autonomous agent then drives through a real EDA toolchain from RTL to GDSII [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA].

### The Silicon ADMET Funnel

This is a constraint inversion. Historically, architecture flowed top-down from intent to RTL and RTL to physical design. Today, physical limitations like thermal envelopes, wire delay, and routing congestion constrain architectural choices bottom-up.

Like drug discovery, finding a high-performance design is often easier than passing these inverted physical limits, what we might call silicon ADMET, borrowing the drug-discovery ADMET screen[^fn-admet-c06] that filters candidate compounds on downstream physical viability rather than potency alone. The multi-fidelity ladder screens candidates by evaluation cost; the same filtering recurs along the physical axis, where data movement, thermal limits, and routing progressively reject high-scoring candidates that cannot survive signoff (@fig-silicon-admet-funnel). Architecture also faces a sim-to-silicon gap, so the AI must optimize for designs that survive physical variation and tool noise rather than fragile peaks in a proxy score.

[^fn-admet-c06]: **ADMET**: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity, the five downstream viability properties a drug candidate must clear regardless of how potent it is.

![**The "Silicon ADMET" funnel.** Drawing a parallel between the phased, rigorous filtering of drug discovery and the physical signoff funnel in computer architecture, both disciplines must weed out high-scoring "decoys" early using increasingly expensive and faithful evaluations.](images/F5-silicon-admet-funnel){#fig-silicon-admet-funnel fig-alt="Two parallel three-stage funnels. Drug discovery narrows from in-silico screening of ten thousand-plus candidates through in-vitro testing to clinical trials; silicon design narrows from fast ISA simulators through RTL and logic synthesis to physical signoff. An isomorphic-filters arrow links the two columns, and a bottom bar notes that both funnels weed out high-scoring decoys before the expensive high-fidelity stages."}

Different tools therefore return different observations, and the environment cannot afford to blur them together. Physical-design tools make this staged feedback particularly clear. Logic synthesis, placement, routing, and signoff expose different observations and failure modes. The interface must state the stage, raw output, and tool-level status for each return. Each physical-design stage returns its own observation class, failure mode, and tool-level status to preserve, from logic synthesis through signoff (@tbl-eda-stage-interface).

::: {.callout-war-story title="Ariane 5 and the reused alignment module"}
**The claim.** Ariane 5 reused the inertial-reference alignment software from Ariane 4 for its maiden flight [@LionsAriane1996]. The code was flight-proven, so the team carried it over as already validated.

**The gap.** That module converted a 64-bit floating-point horizontal-velocity value into a 16-bit signed integer, a conversion that stayed in range only within Ariane 4's flight profile. Ariane 5 reached horizontal velocities roughly five times higher, the value overflowed, and the conversion raised an unhandled exception. The computation was dead code, needed only for Ariane 4's pre-launch alignment and useless once the vehicle had left the pad, yet it ran anyway and halted an otherwise-healthy inertial navigation system. The rocket self-destructed about 37 seconds after launch.

**The lesson.** The fault lived in the environment, not the intent. The alignment module ran to completion and returned a value; nothing in the flight objective was wrong. What failed was an assumption frozen into a reused component, a numeric range that no longer held once the surrounding vehicle changed. Architecture environments hide the same trap. A tool version, a reused wrapper's operating range, or the meaning of a return can go unrevalidated when the tool or the workload changes, and a run that exits cleanly then propagates a wrong result. The interface has to expose those assumptions so each study rechecks them against its own conditions rather than inheriting them on faith.
:::

| **EDA stage** | **Observation returned** | **Problem it can reveal** | **Tool-level outcome to preserve** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Logic synthesis** | Mapped gates, area estimates, timing estimates, constraint warnings, and early power estimates. | Nonsynthesizable RTL, impossible constraints, and early area or timing problems. | A completed report, including declared constraint failures, is a valid observation; failure to produce the report is a tool-path failure. |
| **Floorplanning and placement** | Cell locations, utilization, congestion hints, timing pressure, and macro or memory placement effects. | Floorplans that create severe congestion, timing pressure, or integration problems. | Congestion or timing violations are valid observations from this stage, while an unsupported floorplan state remains out of scope. |
| **Clock, routing, and power closure** | Routed timing, clock behavior, congestion, design-rule checks, power integrity, and closure failures. | Physical effects absent from earlier tool stages. | Preserve each reported violation and warning separately from a timeout, license failure, or broken run. |
| **Signoff analysis** | Signoff reports, warning classes, violations, analysis conditions, and waived tool messages. | Conditions that remain unresolved at the end of the declared physical tool path. | Record the report and tool outcome without treating the tool status as an architecture decision. |

: **EDA stages return different findings.** From logic synthesis through signoff, each physical-design stage can reveal different candidate problems. To prevent AI hallucination, the environment must strictly map the output of the specific stage to the appropriate semantic meaning, never conflating an early synthesis estimate with a final signoff violation. {#tbl-eda-stage-interface tbl-colwidths="[20,25,25,30]"}

To balance determinism versus reproducibility, we must consider costs, operational fidelity, nondeterminism, and integrity. Two post-route attempts for the same hardware artifact may differ because of seed, thread count, host state, or tool heuristics. To manage nondeterminism and flakiness, distinguish three cases: expected statistical variation, declared tool nondeterminism, and flaky/unstable execution. Do not silently average contradictory returns from different stages, sources, or attempts.

Software engineering benchmarks like SWE-bench demonstrate that loosely connected scripts lead to unreproducible outcomes, so an AI needs explicit read, action, and return paths to avoid generating false positives. Architecture 2.0 must adopt the same discipline for tool execution, enforcing strict data provenance and reproducible environment snapshots. Much like modern cloud DevOps relies on immutable infrastructure, declaring a new state rather than manually patching a running server, architecture environments must enforce *immutable architecture states*.

Mutating a source file in place often corrupts the working directory when an EDA tool crashes. Rather than have the AI patch the broken directory with `sed`, early exploration actions branch from a pristine, immutable snapshot. However, always restarting from pristine RTL source is economically unviable in the deeper stages of the Silicon ADMET funnel, where physical design runs take days and generate gigabytes of intermediate databases. Thus, the environment must support **incremental physical checkpoints**, allowing the agent to branch from intermediate physical states (e.g., post-placement databases) for local optimization.

## Beyond the Synchronous `env.step()` Loop

The standard machine learning loop assumes a synchronous `env.step()` function, where the agent takes a discrete action and the simulation instantly returns the new state and a reward. Because surviving the bottom of the Silicon ADMET funnel requires physical layout runs that take days to complete, this synchronous paradigm structurally fails. The Simulator Tax shows up here in practice. An agent waiting for a synchronous `env.step()` could wait 8 hours for a physical routing failure in an EDA tool, compared to the 10 milliseconds it takes to receive a Python syntax error in a software environment. A physical synthesis flow cannot be driven through a blocking call, which will time out or hang when a placement job takes 40 hours or waits three days for an EDA license checkout.

Synchrony is only the most visible assumption this tutorial abstraction imports. Gym also assumes a cheap reset, yet an architecture environment has none; branching from a pristine snapshot is the closest equivalent, and every branch still pays real build and simulation cost. It assumes a Markov[^fn-markov-property-c06] step whose outcome depends only on the action, but EDA tools carry hidden cross-call state in caches, working directories, and license servers, which breaks the Markov assumption. It also expects a dense scalar reward after every step, whereas architectural feedback is sparse, arriving only at the end of a long chain of builds and checks, which leaves a poor final result hard to attribute to any single upstream action.

[^fn-markov-property-c06]: **Markov property**: The assumption that an environment's next state depends only on the current state and the chosen action, never on the longer history of how the system arrived there. Hidden cross-call state violates it, which is why stateless-looking tool wrappers mislead learning methods.

Each of these gaps has to be engineered away in the harness rather than the learning algorithm. The harness, not the agent that acts against it, is the deliverable.

Real tool chains require asynchronous, scarce, and protected execution mechanics. Long simulations, FPGA builds, EDA stages, and signoff require explicit submit, poll, resume, cancel, timeout, retry, queue, license, permission, artifact-isolation, and partial-return behavior. These are architecture environment semantics because they determine which candidate ran, which stage completed, which artifacts are valid, and whether another attempt is comparable.

Because returns arrive asynchronously and sometimes days late, omitting asynchronous state breaks the learning loop. From an ML-Sys perspective, the environment's "State" must dynamically include **in-flight jobs and queue depth**. If an agent dispatches 50 parallel multi-day EDA jobs and the environment hides this pending state, the agent's policy will suffer from *action-collapse*, spamming identical redundant actions because it has no visibility into the queued work. Furthermore, the environment must stream **intermediate surrogate rewards**. The interface should emit partial observations as the job progresses (e.g., logic synthesis complete, initial timing estimates). This allows the RL agent to perform early trajectory pruning rather than waiting three days for a final binary routing failure.

A critical requirement of this asynchronous system is explicitly distinguishing between an **infrastructure failure** and an **architectural constraint violation**. If an AI proposes an SRAM configuration and the simulator crashes due to a host Out-Of-Memory (OOM) error, or because a license server went offline, this is an infrastructure failure. If the AI is penalized for this attempt, its policy will spuriously down-weight the SRAM configuration, polluting the design space exploration with infrastructure noise.

| **Failure type** | **Symptom** | **Environment action** | **Architectural meaning** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Infrastructure failure | Host out of memory, EDA license checkout timeout, cluster node crash. | Flag as `RETRY_ELIGIBLE` or `TOOL_CRASH`. | None. The candidate remains untested and must not be penalized in the design space. |
| Architectural constraint | Negative timing slack, unroutable netlist congestion, thermal violation > 3 W. | Flag as valid evaluation return. | Negative design feedback. The candidate is physically infeasible and should be rejected or penalized. |

: **Cluster flakiness must never penalize a candidate:** When a host crash or license timeout aborts a run, the candidate remains untested and must not be down-weighted in the design space. The environment harness must trap infrastructure failures and handle them separately from true physical design constraints. {#tbl-failure-taxonomy tbl-colwidths="[20,30,25,25]"}

The environment harness must catch infrastructure failures and flag them appropriately (@tbl-failure-taxonomy), preventing the agent from optimizing against false negative signals. Only true architectural failures, such as failing to meet a timing constraint in synthesis or causing a thermal violation in the system's 3 W envelope, should be passed back to the AI as negative design feedback.

Some tool crashes, however, carry real architectural signal. A pathological candidate can exhaust host memory, prove unroutable, or fail synthesis because its own resource footprint is infeasible rather than because the cluster is at fault. The harness cannot always separate the two before running, so it needs a retry-with-fingerprint rule. If the same candidate crashes the same tool in the same way across repeated attempts, the harness reclassifies the outcome from `TOOL_CRASH` to an architectural infeasibility signal.

However, merely returning a generic "failed" signal deprives the agent of architectural feedback. When a tool crashes (such as a router OOM due to an unroutable netlist), the environment wrapper should defensively parse *intermediate* or partial outputs—like the last successful placement density map—to synthesize a negative architectural reward. By converting an uninformative infrastructure crash back into actionable design feedback, the agent parses the specific failure mode. To navigate this sparse architectural feedback, the environment must also formulate rewards as multi-objective Pareto-dominance signals (explicitly balancing Power, Performance, and Area) rather than a single scalar, enabling the agent to learn the physical trade-off frontier.

## The Three-Path Interface

A tool returns raw, unstructured text, but an architecture study needs structured observations it can compare, check, and store. Turning one into the other is the job of the environment interface.

![**The architecture environment interface.** An architecture environment connects a system intent to legal actions and translates raw tool outputs into semantic observations. The wrapper checks the request, calls the tool, and parses the result, while the harness records the run and its provenance.](images/F6-environment-tool-interface){#fig-environment-tool-interface fig-alt="A diagram showing how an architecture environment connects an architecture question and workload, an action schema, and declared constraints and metric definitions to a wrapper and harness."}

An architecture environment explicitly maps intent to actions and actions to observations (@fig-environment-tool-interface). The wrapper acts as a protective boundary, intercepting high-level requests, validating them via the read path, executing tool commands via the action path, and distilling logs into a semantic vector via the return path.

### Defending Against Reward Hacking

The machine learning community has long warned of *reward hacking* [@AmodeiEtAl2016Concrete], a modern instance of Goodhart's Law[^fn-goodharts-law-c06] [@Strathern1997Goodhart; @Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement]. Given a simple scalar reward, an AI may exploit the objective function to maximize that number while violating physical constraints [@OpenAIClark2016FaultyRewards]. In architecture, reward hacking manifests as physically impossible designs. If an environment merely reports IPC without constraints, the AI might propose a 10-terabyte L1 cache to maximize the score.

::: {.callout-war-story title="Reward hacking the IPC proxy"}
**The claim.** In an early automated design space exploration study, an optimization agent was rewarded purely for maximizing Instructions Per Cycle (IPC) on a suite of benchmarks.

**The gap.** The optimizer maximized this proxy metric by proposing a physically impossible structure—a 100-port SRAM cache. The design looked brilliant in functional simulation, achieving unprecedented IPC, but was immediately rejected by physical synthesis due to catastrophic wire routing congestion and impossible area requirements.

**The lesson.** Proxy metrics like IPC are easily exploited if not bounded by physical reality. The environment must enforce the downstream constraints of the Silicon ADMET funnel to prevent an AI from proposing structures that cannot exist in silicon.
:::

[^fn-goodharts-law-c06]: **Goodhart's Law**: The observation, originally from monetary economics, that when a measure becomes an optimization target it stops being a good measure. An optimizer rewarded on a proxy metric maximizes the proxy, not the goal the proxy once tracked.

Because physical design limits dictate architectural choices bottom-up, ground truth from traditional EDA tools is our only defense against these AI exploits. It remains indispensable for enforcing laws like timing closure and power limits.

### Formalizing the Paths

To make this data usable, the environment establishes three distinct paths:

1. **The Read Path:** This supplies state references, fixed context, permissions, and economic budgets (e.g., cluster hours under the Slurm workload manager) *before* an action is proposed. This allows the agent to balance the fidelity of its proposed action against the cost of execution. The environment must explicitly contrast the trivial compute cost of AI token inference against the much larger economic cost of the target EDA simulation.
2. **The Action Path:** To prevent unsafe or nonsensical proposals, the Action Path exposes a *safe-by-construction* action space. However, architectural parameters are rarely independent (e.g., cache capacity, block size, and associativity dictate if the number of sets is valid; memory timings have strict inter-dependencies). The environment wrapper must act as a **constraint solver**, intercepting algebraically invalid combinations *before* invoking the simulator. By projecting the AI's independent mutations onto a strictly legal hardware manifold, it prevents the AI from proposing physically impossible states.
3. **The Return Path:** This carries typed tool returns, raw artifacts, cost, latency, provenance, and terminal outcomes. To manage micro-architectural nondeterminism (like OS thread scheduling or asynchronous I/O noise in full-system simulators), the environment must orchestrate multiple statistical samples. Instead of returning a single noisy scalar IPC, the environment should return a *confidence interval*, forcing the AI to optimize for robust architectural gains rather than exploiting statistical artifacts.

An agent's action space can range from simple parameter tuning to complex structural mutations (like rewriting an MLIR dataflow graph). By encapsulating these within a formalized read/action cycle, the environment protects the physical infrastructure from rogue agent behaviors.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
Rather than providing raw Python code, we can also formalize the overall execution loop as a standard algorithmic interface (@lst-environment-interface), drawing inspiration from frameworks like OpenAI Gymnasium but tailored for the unique constraints of hardware design [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium].
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
Rather than providing raw Python code, we can also formalize the overall execution loop as a standard algorithmic interface (Algorithm~\ref{lst-environment-interface}), drawing inspiration from frameworks like OpenAI Gymnasium but tailored for the unique constraints of hardware design [@TowersEtAl2023Gymnasium].
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
```{=latex}
\begin{algorithm}[H]
\caption{\textbf{One validated action becomes one recorded run:} the interface rejects illegal actions before touching a tool, submits work asynchronously, separates infrastructure crashes from architectural failures, and returns a typed observation with provenance.}\label{lst-environment-interface}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require \texttt{action\_request} (e.g., target L2 cache size, routing effort)
\Ensure \texttt{observation\_vector}, \texttt{status\_flags}, \texttt{provenance\_metadata}
\State \textbf{Validate Action (Read/Action Path):}
\If{\texttt{action\_request} violates fixed constraints}
    \State \Return \texttt{INVALID\_ACTION} immediately. Do not invoke tools.
\EndIf
\State \textbf{Translate to Tool Commands:}
\State Lower \texttt{action\_request} into tool-specific configurations.
\State \textbf{Asynchronous Execution (Return Path):}
\State \texttt{job\_id} $\gets$ \text{Submit job to cluster/queue.}
\State \Return \texttt{PENDING(job\_id)} immediately.
\State \dots \textit{Later, upon polling \texttt{job\_id}:} \dots
\If{infrastructure fails (timeout, missing license)}
    \State \Return \texttt{TOOL\_CRASH}. Do not penalize the architecture candidate.
\EndIf
\State \textbf{Data Distillation:}
\State Parse the tool stdout and trace files.
\State Extract KPIs into \texttt{observation\_vector}.
\State \textbf{Return State:}
\State Package \texttt{observation\_vector}, \texttt{status\_flags}, and exact tool hashes.
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {#lst-environment-interface .algorithm lst-cap="**One validated action becomes one recorded run:** the interface rejects illegal actions before touching a tool, submits work asynchronously, separates infrastructure crashes from architectural failures, and returns a typed observation with provenance."}
**Require:** `action_request`
**Ensure:** `observation_vector`, `status_flags`, `provenance_metadata`

1. **Validate Action (Read/Action Path):**

   - If `action_request` violates fixed constraints:
     - **return** `INVALID_ACTION` immediately. Do not invoke tools.
2. **Translate to Tool Commands:**

   - Lower `action_request` into tool-specific configurations (e.g., CACTI `.cfg`).
3. **Asynchronous Execution (Return Path):**

   - Submit job to cluster/queue and obtain `job_id`.
   - **return** `PENDING(job_id)` immediately.
   - *... Later, upon polling the `job_id` status ...*
   - If infrastructure fails:
     - **return** `TOOL_CRASH`. Do not penalize candidate.
4. **Data Distillation:**

   - Parse tool stdout and trace files.
   - Extract KPIs into `observation_vector`.
5. **Return State:**

   - Package `observation_vector`, `status_flags`, and exact tool hashes.
:::
:::

Distinct read, action, and return paths let an architecture environment carry architectural intent across domain boundaries, from the compiler's intermediate representation to the final physical design signoff. The environment stops short of making the architectural decision, which keeps it a trusted observation platform.

If another method can act in the same harness and another architect can interpret its results without private knowledge, the environment is sound. Generative models and optimization algorithms can then operate on the environment independently.

The Return Path is where a raw tool log becomes the observation the agent acts on. But capturing the return safely is only the first step; we must also ensure the AI can parse it.

## Attention Bottlenecks and Distillation

When interfacing AI models with traditional architecture tools, a mismatch occurs at the observation layer. A commercial EDA tool or a detailed simulator like gem5 generates exhaustive text output, often containing tens of thousands of lines. If an environment wrapper naively pipes raw stdout directly back to an AI, the agent will struggle to isolate relevant signals from the noise, making it harder to debug the actual hardware issue.

A critical requirement of the Return Path is **Data Distillation**. Because traditional architecture and EDA tools are verbose, the architect must build robust *log-to-semantic parsers* into the environment wrapper.

This creates an asymmetry. We can bound the agent's *input* actions using compiler IRs like CIRCT, but the *output* from legacy EDA tools remains an unstructured stream of text. While modern tools offer clean Python APIs (like OpenROAD), legacy commercial flows rely on Tcl. Crucially, Tcl shells (like `dc_shell`) are stateful, side-effect-heavy REPLs, not clean APIs. The environment wrapper must therefore inject self-trapping scripts (e.g., using `catch`) that serialize their own structured JSON, shielding the agent from Tcl's fragility.

::: {.callout-war-story title="The swallowed synthesis warning"}
**The claim.** A continuous integration (CI) script or parsing regex was tuned to known synthesis errors to catch design-rule violations.

**The gap.** The script silently swallowed a new, unclassified warning about a downgraded timing constraint and a miswired clock domain crossing hidden inside 50,000 lines of log text. Because the regex only flagged what it knew, the error was ignored, resulting in a dead-on-arrival chip.

**The lesson.** Log parsers cannot afford to discard the unknown. This grounds the need to preserve "unclassified anomalies" alongside structured JSON, ensuring that critical but unfamiliar warnings are not filtered away from the agent's attention.
:::

Much like DevOps engineers use monitoring tools to distill millions of server logs into key metrics, architecture environments must translate sprawling outputs into structured summaries. Consider our Lighthouse XR prompt: if the vector accelerator causes a thermal violation, returning the raw 5,000-line power analysis log will immediately hit the LLM's "telemetry wall" and exhaust its context window. The environment wrapper must parse the EDA log, filter out irrelevant setup warnings, and distill the thermal violation into a clean JSON observation (e.g., `{"violation": "thermal", "peak_w": 3.4, "budget_w": 3.0}`). Furthermore, for unclassified anomalies that cannot be mapped to a simple schema, the parser must apply mechanical truncation and semantic filtering (e.g., extracting the last 50 lines before a FATAL tag). This preserves the actionable failure string without overflowing the context window.

Distillation must preserve, not discard, unclassified anomalies. A parser tuned to known design-rule violations can silently drop the swapped library corner, downgraded constraint, or version-deprecation notice that a brownfield debug actually turns on. A safer wrapper returns two channels, a structured vector of the recognized metrics and violations alongside a flagged residual of the unparsed warning and error lines plus an integrity hash of the full log, so the agent gets a dense observation without the harness deciding on its own that a warning was irrelevant.

Representing a tool like Yosys or OpenROAD for an agent involves defining its input schema (e.g., accepted flags, valid file formats, constraint objects), its execution bounds, and its structured outputs (e.g., JSON-formatted area and timing reports rather than raw text stdout). However, agents eventually hit a telemetry wall, because context windows restrict how much output they can observe. When an API serializes a large physical layout into text, it risks lossy serialization.

Truncating a million-line timing trace to fit a context window creates a permanent verification blind spot for the AI, causing it to falsely predict success because the error was paginated away. Formalizing tools as typed APIs with explicit failure modes and hierarchical summarization lets the agent programmatically construct valid toolchain requests. It parses the resulting metrics directly into its internal state, executing deterministic recovery actions without hitting the telemetry wall. The architect ultimately reviews these structured summaries in the evaluation harness to ensure thermal budgets and STA hold.

## Hardware API Standardization

While a robust three-path interface manages execution, the payloads traversing those paths must be mathematically and structurally unambiguous. Historically, hardware descriptions relied on fragmented, vendor-specific languages (like SystemVerilog) built for human designers and proprietary logic synthesizers, not programmatic mutation.

If an AI agent relies on text-based string-matching or shallow Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) parsing to modify a Verilog module, it will corrupt the design. Textual regex cannot safely resolve tangled macro expansions, evaluate parameterized `generate` blocks, or infer the unspoken module hierarchies that ultimately dictate physical placement and routing.

This brittleness necessitates the *Standardization of Hardware APIs* through open, formally structured intermediary representations, most notably MLIR (Multi-Level Intermediate Representation) and its hardware-centric counterpart CIRCT (Circuit IR Compilers and Tools).

CIRCT replaces unstructured text with a strict, queryable Static Single Assignment (SSA)[^fn-ssa-c06] form that explicitly models dataflow, concurrency, and structural dependencies.

[^fn-ssa-c06]: **Static Single Assignment (SSA)**: A compiler intermediate form in which every value is defined exactly once and never reassigned, so a program's dataflow is explicit in its structure. For hardware, this is what makes an IR graph traversable and checkable in a way raw Verilog text is not. CIRCT captures hardware intent as a graph of progressive dialects, stepping down from high-level abstractions (`firrtl` or `handshake`) to structural nets (`hw` and `comb`), which gives AI agents a typed, deterministic interface.

Instead of blind text mutation, an agent can programmatically walk the SSA graph to inject a pipeline register or re-balance a datapath, relying on the compiler framework to enforce semantic legality by construction.

For the human architect, these standardized representations form an indispensable safety boundary. They ensure the AI's intent survives translation across the physical toolchain, and they rule out structurally illegal states by construction. Physical realizability is a separate question, and it still comes from the downstream tools that measure timing, power, and congestion.

## Orchestrating Complex Toolchains

When a candidate design successfully navigates the Three-Path Interface and its intent is safely encoded in a standardized IR like MLIR, it must be translated into actionable physical tool commands. However, a single high-level intent rarely maps to a single tool. A hardware configuration might need to fan out to multiple distinct evaluation backends. These include an RTL simulator for functional correctness, a VLSI flow for power and area estimates, and an FPGA emulation path for full-stack software booting.

![**The Chipyard framework.** Chipyard, an open-source RISC-V SoC generator, routes a single configuration downward to three backend evaluation paths: RTL simulation, VLSI flow, and FPGA emulation. This fan-out ensures one configuration reaches every evaluation path consistently.](images/F6b-chipyard-framework){#fig-chipyard-framework fig-alt="A flow diagram of the Chipyard SoC-generation framework. A configuration system feeds Chisel generators (Rocket, BOOM, Hwacha) into the FIRRTL compiler, which fans the single configuration out to three backend paths: RTL simulation, a VLSI flow, and FPGA emulation."}

The environment framework routes one candidate architecture change downward into several legal tool actions without losing its connection to the system intent (@fig-chipyard-framework).

### Declarative Execution Planning

To manage this fan-out, we must look to adjacent domains that have solved this exact problem of decoupling *intent* from *messy execution mechanics*.

In Database Query Optimization, a software engineer declares *what* data they want via a SQL query, never specifying *how* to read the disk or which B-tree to traverse. A query planner analyzes the request, checks its cached data, evaluates the compute budget, and builds an optimal execution plan dynamically. Similarly, an architecture environment can act as a query planner for evaluations. Instead of the AI imperatively calling a specific simulator script, it should issue a declarative hypothesis: `Evaluate(Candidate=Lighthouse_V2, Metric=IPC)`. The environment then determines whether to serve a cached result, query a fast analytical model, or provision a 24-hour RTL simulation based on the current budget constraints.

In computational biology, executing a genomic pipeline previously required brittle bash scripts. Frameworks like Nextflow [@DiTommasoEtAl2017Nextflow] and Snakemake [@KosterEtAl2012Snakemake] emerged to formalize dataflow, isolating the *scientific logic* from the *execution mechanics* (cluster queues, retries, and tool crashes). In cloud computing, Kubernetes relies on desired-state reconciliation. The user declares the intent, and the orchestration engine handles the low-level failures. These frameworks abstract execution mechanics into a formal graph, letting the architect review high-level declarative goals instead of debugging why a synthesis job crashed on node 4.

Architecture 2.0 environments must act as this orchestration layer. A semantic proposal may require several reads, transformations, builds, executions, and checks. Their dependencies form a graph rather than a single call or mandatory sequence.

Fulfilling the Lighthouse prompt for a complex System-on-Chip (SoC) means orchestrating the design intent through the Chipyard generator framework as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of dependencies. Integrating the low-power RISC-V compute subsystem with custom XR accelerators requires explicit lowering from MLIR to RTL, along with related compiler IR transformations. The dataflow moves through several precise stages. An agent's high-level intent first triggers an MLIR lowering to emit new spatial-tracking instructions, which then informs a hardware target feature declaration within the Chipyard configuration.

That configuration fans out into multiple execution branches. It generates RTL, which in turn feeds both a rebuilt custom Linux binary for a functional correctness run in Verilator, an open-source RTL simulator, and a physical logic synthesis flow that checks routing congestion and verifies the power budget. The environment acts as the arbiter of this DAG, running some branches in parallel while others block until earlier artifacts exist, so the AI's edits are vetted against physical realities before they are presented back for review.

### Sandbox Resilience

EDA tools and cycle-accurate simulators are notoriously brittle, slow, and expensive to run. Safe exploration isn't just about AI safety; it's about not crashing the simulation host. The architecture environment must act as a resilient sandbox. It isolates tool execution, enforces strict timeout budgets on generated RTL (to catch infinite loops), and safely interprets tool panics or segmentation faults without losing its contextual train of thought.

### Artifact Lineage and Provenance

To illustrate this orchestration complexity, consider how a single architecture proposal formally splits into specific software and hardware instantiations (@fig-artifact-lineage).

![**Artifact lineage and cryptographic provenance.** A single Lighthouse intent fans out into software binaries and hardware RTL, each hashed to ensure reproducible evaluations.](images/F5-artifact-lineage){#fig-artifact-lineage fig-alt="Artifact Lineage and Cryptographic Provenance. A single Lighthouse intent fans out into software binaries and hardware RTL, each hashed to ensure reproducible evaluations."}

Software variant S2 may be an MLIR-derived lowering compiled into binary B2. Hardware variant H3 may be a Chipyard-derived configuration elaborated into RTL R3. Changing B2 while holding R3 fixed creates a new evaluation instance even if the root proposal is unchanged.

An evaluation instance binds every layer relevant to that tool action. Each transformation records parent, tool and transformation version, input identifiers, output identifiers, content hashes where useful, and the intended semantic relation. A semantics-changing edit creates a child candidate. Google's Bazel [@Bazel] build system guarantees reproducibility by enforcing hermeticity, where every output is a strict cryptographic hash of its inputs. This matches the architectural need to track hardware candidate identity as it lowers from a C++ memory model to RTL to Layout. A hash proves artifact identity, not architectural or functional equivalence.

## Open Research Questions

Integrating autonomous agents with legacy EDA workflows raises several open problems, from building programmatic abstractions over proprietary foundry tools, to running those tools asynchronously and safely, to tracing a physical sign-off violation back to the upstream mutation that caused it.

**Theme 1: The EDA Abstraction Layer.** Agents need a uniform programmatic interface over proprietary tools that were built for humans reading log files, not for APIs.

- How can we build programmatic wrappers that give an AI agent a uniform interface over fragmented, proprietary vendor tools?
- What observation schema captures the state of a proprietary synthesis run well enough for an open-source agent to act on it?
- Can open IRs like CIRCT cover enough of a real vendor flow to replace brittle text mutation with structured, verifiable edits?

**Theme 2: Secure and Asynchronous Execution.** Real tool feedback arrives slowly and out of order, and the action space has to stay safe across tools without hand-coding every limit.

- What makes an action space safe by construction across many vendor tools, so an agent cannot propose physically impossible states without hand-coding each tool's limits?
- How must an agent maintain state and context when synthesis feedback takes days to arrive and returns out of order?
- What harness rules can separate an infrastructure failure from a true architectural constraint violation before a candidate is penalized?

**Theme 3: Bridging the Sim-to-Silicon Gap.** A design can pass every simulation and still fail in silicon.

- What models can trace a late-stage physical sign-off violation back to the upstream RTL mutation that caused it?
- How can an environment detect when an agent is exploiting a physical dimension its current simulator fidelity cannot verify?
- How can verbose EDA logs be distilled into a dense observation without discarding the unclassified anomalies a brownfield debug depends on?

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="The Action Space Must Not Exceed Oracle Fidelity"}
Never allow an agent to propose architectural changes that the available simulator or formal tool cannot verify. If an AI mutates a thermal property but the EDA loop only runs logic simulation, the agent will silently exploit the unchecked dimension. The permitted action space must be strictly bounded by the physical dimensions the feedback budget can measure.
:::


An architecture environment transforms opaque tool executions into an explicit interface that AI methods and human architects can trust. It records precisely which tensor-enabled software artifact ran against which hardware artifact, exactly which tools completed, which actions failed or lacked support, and the typed meaning of every return.

A well-maintained environment is the contract that makes AI-driven architectural discovery reproducible, auditable, and physically valid.

::: {.callout-carry-forward}
- **Carry forward:** An architecture environment exposes a read, action, and return interface so a candidate change reaches legal tool actions and every raw tool output becomes a typed observation another architect can inspect.
- **Reader test:** Can another method act in the same harness, and another architect interpret its returns, without private knowledge from whoever built the environment?
- **Up next:** The loop can now represent state, propose changes, and execute them against real tools. But when the environment returns an observation (a passing DRC, a failed synthesis run, a timing report), how do we know we can trust it? In @sec-feedback-verification-trust, we take up the foundation of the Evaluate stage: how raw observations become rigorous feedback, verified claims, and architectural trust.
:::
